name: OPA1612AIDR
title: OPA1611 and OPA1612: low-noise, low-distortion bipolar-input audio op amps
summary: The OPA1611 is a single and the OPA1612 a dual op amp for audio, with bipolar inputs, 1.1 nV/√Hz voltage noise at 1 kHz and THD+N of 0.000015 % at 1 kHz. They run from ±2.25 V to ±18 V (4.5 V to 36 V total) at 3.6 mA per channel, are stable at unity gain, give 40 MHz gain bandwidth and 27 V/µs slew, and the output swings to within 600 mV of either rail into 2 kΩ with ±30 mA of drive. Each channel of the dual is built separately so the two do not interact, even when one is overdriven.

circuits.title: Audio DAC post filter (I/V converter and low-pass filter)
circuits.description: Left channel of a headphone-grade output stage behind an audio DAC whose outputs are a differential pair of currents; the right channel is a second copy. U1 and U2 are current-to-voltage converters, each with its DAC output on the inverting input and 820 Ω of feedback, with 2200 pF across each feedback resistor rolling off the top end. U3 takes the difference of the two converter outputs through 680 Ω and 620 Ω resistors, with 8200 pF across the pair of midpoints, 330 Ω and 2700 pF on each side, giving a single-ended low-pass output. U3's output reaches the jack through 100 Ω. Every supply pin has 0.1 µF to ground and the rails are ±15 V.

circuits.title: Distortion test circuit
circuits.description: The op amp is set up as a non-inverting amplifier of signal gain 1 + R2/R1, with a small R3 between the two inputs. R3 lowers the loop gain without changing the signal gain, so the amplifier's distortion appears 1 + R2/(R1 || R3) times larger at the output, lifting it above the analyzer's floor; the input signal and the load the part sees stay those of the plain amplifier. Part values are the G = +10 settings (distortion gain 110); the G = +1 and G = -1 settings are listed under distortion test circuit settings.

operation.text: OPA1611 is one amplifier, in SOIC-8. OPA1612 is two amplifiers, in SOIC-8 or a 3 mm × 3 mm SON-8 with an exposed pad. The two channels of the OPA1612 have fully separate circuitry, for low crosstalk and no interaction even when one channel is overdriven or overloaded. An automotive-qualified version, OPA1612-Q1, also exists.

Both parts are stable at unity gain and the output does not reverse phase. The output swings to 600 mV of either rail into 2 kΩ and 200 mV into 10 kΩ, and the input common-mode range stops 2 V inside each rail.

Operation is from 4.5 V to 36 V across the supplies (±2.25 V to ±18 V). The two rails need not be equal: +25 V with -5 V is one example. The input common-mode voltage must stay within its specified range in every case. Guaranteed parameters hold from -40 °C to +85 °C; behaviour with supply and temperature is in the typical curves. Above 40 V across the supplies the part can be damaged for good.

Put 0.1 µF low-ESR ceramic capacitors from each supply pin to ground, close to the part; with one supply a single capacitor from V+ to ground does. Noisy or high-impedance supplies especially call for them.

The parts can drive 2 kΩ loads from ±18 V, and dissipation inside rises with supply voltage. A copper lead frame carries heat out better than ordinary materials; wide copper traces on the board act as extra heat sink, and soldering the part in rather than socketing it keeps junction temperature lower.

Back-to-back diodes across the inputs limit the differential input voltage. They do nothing in most circuits, but in low gain or unity gain a fast input edge can outrun the output and turn the diodes on (Figure 17 shows the effect). Input current must then be held to 10 mA or less, by a series input resistor RI or a feedback resistor RF if the source does not limit it; a series input resistor adds noise.

Steering diodes run from each input and the output to internal supply lines, which meet at an edge-triggered absorption clamp across the supplies; a fast ESD pulse across the supply pins fires the clamp and holds the voltage safe, and the energy ends as heat. In normal operation none of this conducts. If an input is driven 500 mV or more above +VS, an upper steering diode carries current into +VS; keep that input current to 10 mA. If +VS cannot sink it, the input can end up powering the amplifier and pull the rail past the absolute maximum, and in rare cases the clamp can latch on across live supplies, conducting directly between them and destroying the part. A signal applied while the supplies sit at 0 V either powers the amplifier through the diodes (high-impedance supplies) or drives large diode current limited only by the source and its series resistance (low-impedance supplies). Where the supply may not absorb such current, zener diodes from the supply pins can be added, chosen to stay off in normal running but to conduct before the rail reaches an unsafe level.

The amplifier's voltage noise acts as a varying offset and its current noise as a varying bias current that turns into voltage across the source resistance; total noise is the root sum of squares of source, amplifier and feedback-network noise. When the source impedance is small, the current-noise term hardly matters and the voltage noise sets the total, which is why these parts fit sources under 1 kΩ. In a gain stage the feedback resistors add thermal noise and turn the current noise into voltage; their values can usually be picked to make both terms negligible.

THD+N stays below 0.00008 % from 20 Hz to 20 kHz at G = +1, 3 VRMS, 80 kHz bandwidth and 2 kΩ load. Distortion this low is below many analyzers' floor, so the test circuit raises it by reducing the loop gain with a small resistor across the inputs; keep that resistor small so it barely affects the measurement. Repeating a reading at high gain or high frequency, where the analyzer can resolve the distortion directly, confirms the method.

Low closed-loop gain combined with heavy capacitive load erodes phase margin and can bring gain peaking or oscillation. Isolate large capacitive loads with a small series output resistor, 50 Ω for instance; it also limits dissipation if the output is shorted. Figures 19 and 20 give overshoot against load capacitance for several series resistors.

Bypass each supply pin to ground with low-ESR 0.1 µF ceramics placed as near the part as possible. Keep analog and digital grounds apart and watch where ground current flows; a ground plane on one or more layers spreads heat and cuts EMI pickup. Route input traces away from supply and output traces, crossing noisy traces at right angles rather than running alongside. Keep external parts close to the part, with RF and RG right at the inverting input to keep its parasitic capacitance down, and keep input traces short since they are the most sensitive nodes. A driven low-impedance guard ring around critical traces cuts leakage from neighbouring traces at other potentials.
The SON-8 underside pad connects to V-. It must be soldered to the board for heat removal, mechanical strength and specified performance.
